topic: Lawful basis attaches to purpose, not to tooling
stem: A Nordic energy retailer is launching a Claude-based billing assistant for its 1.8 million domestic customers. The assistant answers questions about the customer's own consumption and invoices, and the team also wants to retain transcripts for six months to tune prompts. The DPO must record a lawful basis before go-live. The product manager argues that consent should be collected on first use because 'consent is always the safest option'. Which analysis should the architect support?

options.text: Basis follows purpose, not tooling: a query about the customer's own bill sits under the basis recorded for servicing the supply contract, while retaining transcripts to tune prompts is a separate purpose with its own basis and record entry.

Consent must be captured on first use through a dialog the customer accepts before the chat opens, because introducing a new processing technology into an existing service resets the basis for the whole interaction.

No fresh assessment is required, because the model provider acts as a processor under a data processing agreement and the retailer's existing basis for the billing relationship therefore extends to everything the assistant does with the data.

A single legitimate interests assessment should cover the assistant end to end, with one balancing test carrying both the service-delivery use and the six-month transcript retention as a single entry in the processing record.

explanation.correct: The stem describes two different purposes wearing one interface. Answering a customer's own billing question is the service the customer contracted for; swapping a search page for a Claude assistant changes the mechanism, not the purpose, so the recorded basis for servicing the contract still carries it. Retaining six months of transcripts to improve a product is a separate purpose with a different beneficiary, and it needs its own basis, its own retention justification and its own line in the record of processing. Splitting them also keeps the service working if a customer objects to the secondary use.

distractors.B: Consent is not a default upgrade. It must be freely given and withdrawable, and offering a choice the retailer will override anyway - it still has to bill the customer - makes the consent invalid and the notice misleading. New technology does not by itself create a consent trigger.
distractors.C: A processor agreement governs how a vendor may handle data on the controller's behalf. It is not a source of lawful basis, and it says nothing about whether a new purpose is permitted. Controllers stay accountable for basis regardless of how tightly the processor is contracted.
distractors.D: One balancing test cannot span two purposes with different risk profiles and different benefit distributions. Bundling them produces an assessment that is unfalsifiable, and it hides the fact that service delivery has a better-fitting basis than legitimate interests in the first place.

explanation.concept: Lawful basis is a property of a processing purpose, not of a system, a vendor or a technology. When an AI feature is introduced into an existing service, decompose it into purposes first: the primary service purpose usually inherits the existing basis, while secondary uses such as tuning, evaluation and analytics are separate purposes requiring their own basis, notice and retention rule.
explanation.tip: When a stem mentions both 'answers the customer's question' and 'we also keep the transcripts for X', it is testing purpose decomposition. Any option that treats the feature as a single monolithic processing activity is the wrong one.

topic: Propagating an erasure request across derived stores
stem: A German insurtech runs a Claude assistant over customer correspondence. The architecture holds: the source correspondence in a document store, chunk text plus embeddings in a vector index, a prompt cache keyed on rendered context, ninety days of request and response payloads in a third-party observability platform, and a weekly frozen evaluation snapshot sampled from real traffic. A customer submits an erasure request that the legal team has confirmed is valid. What should the architect implement?

options.text: Delete the source correspondence from the document store and let the next scheduled full index rebuild remove the derived vectors and chunk text, since embeddings are numerical derivations rather than personal data in their own right.
Remove the customer's name, policy number and contact details from the stored transcripts, which renders the remaining free text anonymous and therefore places it outside the scope of the request.

Delete or re-derive that customer's data in every derived store - index chunks, cached prompts, retained logs and the evaluation snapshot - on a documented internal deadline, with backups handled by restore-time re-deletion.

Hold the request and record that the firm's immutable decision log carries an overriding retention obligation, so no copy of the customer's data anywhere in the platform can be removed while that log exists.

explanation.correct: The stem deliberately lists five places the same personal data now lives. An erasure capability that only touches the system of record is theatre; chunk text in the index still contains the correspondence verbatim, the observability payloads contain both prompt and completion, and the frozen evaluation snapshot is a copy that no production deletion job will ever visit. The answer is a mapped, exercised deletion path across every derived store with a stated completion time, plus a documented position on backups rather than silence about them. That map is also the artefact a supervisory authority will ask to see.

distractors.A: Embeddings and chunk text derived from an identifiable person are generally still personal data, and chunk text is often the original words. Deferring to 'the next full rebuild' also gives no controlled timeline, which is the part a regulator tests when it asks how long erasure actually takes.
distractors.B: Stripping direct identifiers is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation. Correspondence about a specific claim, address or vehicle is frequently re-identifiable from the remaining content, so the record stays in scope and the erasure remains unsatisfied.
distractors.D: There is a genuine tension between immutable audit records and erasure, but it is resolved by scoping - keeping the minimum necessary in the sealed log with a documented legal justification - not by refusing the request across every store. A blanket refusal is the position hardest to defend.

explanation.concept: In an LLM system, personal data fans out into derived representations: chunks, embeddings, caches, trace payloads, eval corpora and backups. Deletion capability must be designed as a mapped fan-out with a stated completion deadline, and every new derived store added to the platform must be registered against that map on the day it is created.
explanation.tip: Count the data stores a stem lists. If it names five and an option touches one, that option is wrong no matter how technically reasonable it sounds. Stems that itemise an architecture in this much detail are telling you the answer is coverage.

topic: What actually triggers a DPIA requirement
stem: Under GDPR, what most directly determines whether a data protection impact assessment is required before an organisation deploys an LLM-based feature?

options.text: Whether any personal data will leave the European Economic Area during inference, prompt caching or trace storage.
Whether the model provider is engaged under contract as a processor rather than as an independent controller.
Whether the volume of personal data processed exceeds the organisation's own internal materiality threshold.
Whether the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, given its nature and scope.

explanation.correct: The trigger is risk to people, assessed from what the processing does and to whom, not from which technology performs it. A high-volume but low-impact use can fall below the threshold, while a small-scale system that scores individuals for an outcome that matters to them can sit well above it. This is why 'we are adding Claude' is never in itself the answer to whether an assessment is needed: an architect has to characterise the processing - profiling, scale, sensitivity of the data, vulnerability of the people affected - before the question can be answered at all.

distractors.A: Cross-border transfer raises its own set of obligations around an appropriate transfer mechanism and assessment, but a transfer is neither necessary nor sufficient for an impact assessment. Purely domestic processing can be high risk, and a routine transfer can be low risk.
distractors.B: Controller and processor roles determine who owes which duties and what the contract must contain. They do not set the assessment threshold; a controller using only in-house infrastructure faces exactly the same test.
distractors.C: Internal materiality thresholds are a useful operational filter for triage, but they are the organisation's own construct. They cannot substitute for the statutory risk test, and a regulator will not accept 'it was below our threshold' as the analysis.

explanation.concept: Impact assessments are triggered by likely high risk to individuals, derived from nature, scope, context and purpose of the processing. Treat AI adoption as a prompt to re-run that test rather than as the test itself, and record the reasoning even when the conclusion is that no full assessment is needed.
explanation.tip: Recall items about compliance triggers usually offer several real obligations as distractors. Ask which one the named artefact is actually gated on, not which ones are also true of the deployment.

topic: Fields required to reconstruct a past model decision
stem: A UK motor insurer must be able to reconstruct any automated claim-triage recommendation its Claude-based system produced, for the whole regulatory retention window. Today the platform stores the model's final output text and a timestamp against the claim reference. Which TWO additions do most to make a past recommendation genuinely reconstructible? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A monthly aggregate report of triage outcomes broken down by product line, region and claim value band.
The exact rendered prompt sent to the model, including the retrieved policy and claim documents and each document's version identifier.
A natural-language rationale that the model is asked to emit alongside each recommendation, explaining why it reached its conclusion.
The resolved model identifier and version, together with the temperature and other decoding parameters used for that call.
The name of the claims handler in every case where a human overrode the system's recommendation, with the date of the override.

explanation.correct: Reconstruction means being able to say what the model was given and how it was configured at that moment. The rendered prompt with versioned retrieved documents captures the input completely, including the retrieval outcome that a later re-run would not reproduce because the index has moved on. The resolved model version and decoding parameters capture the configuration, which matters because a floating alias silently changes what produced the output. With those two fields plus the stored output, the record stands on its own years later; without them the stored output is an assertion with no provenance.

distractors.A: Aggregate outcome reporting supports portfolio monitoring and fairness analysis, and most insurers will want it. It says nothing about any individual recommendation, so it cannot answer a question about a specific claim.
distractors.C: A model-generated rationale is a plausible story produced after the fact, not a trace of the computation. It is useful for human review and for customer communication, but treating it as the audit record means recording something that may be fluent and wrong.
distractors.E: Override records support accountability and are worth keeping, but they only exist for the subset of cases a human changed, and they describe the human's action rather than the model's input. They cannot reconstruct the recommendation itself.

explanation.concept: An AI audit record is reconstructible only if it is self-contained: rendered input, resolved model version, generation parameters, and output. Anything that requires re-executing against live systems - templates, indexes, aliases - has already drifted, so provenance must be captured at write time rather than reassembled at audit time.
explanation.tip: Distinguish 'evidence of what happened' from 'explanation of why'. Model-generated rationales are the most seductive distractor in audit questions because they look exactly like what an auditor wants.

topic: Responding to a regulator request to reproduce an old decision
stem: A Dutch consumer lender receives a request from its supervisory authority to reproduce the Claude-generated affordability summary that supported a specific credit decision made twenty-six months ago. The platform archives full request and response payloads to object storage. However, prompts are assembled at runtime from a template repository that has changed roughly forty times since, and the deployment used a model alias that has been repointed twice. The team has three weeks to respond. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Re-run the archived inputs against the current production configuration and submit the resulting output as the reproduction, noting in the covering letter that generation is non-deterministic.
Inspect the archived payload for that request to establish whether it holds the fully rendered prompt and the resolved model version, since if it does the archive is itself the evidence.

Check out the template repository at the commit tagged nearest the decision date, rebuild the prompt from that template and the stored variable values, and submit the rebuilt prompt as the reproduction.
Open a support case asking the model provider to retrieve the original completion from its own side, so the response can be corroborated by an independent party.

explanation.correct: Before doing any work, establish what the archive already proves. If the stored payload is the rendered prompt rather than a template reference, and the response record carries the resolved model version, then the firm can show exactly what was presented and what came back - which is what the authority is asking for. Re-execution against a probabilistic system produces a different artefact and quietly reframes the question as 'what would the model say today'. This first step also determines everything after it: if the payload turns out to be a template reference, the team knows immediately that it has a much harder reconstruction problem and only three weeks to solve it.

distractors.A: Submitting a fresh generation as a reproduction misrepresents the record. The model version has changed twice and the output is non-deterministic, so any difference between the two is uninterpretable and any similarity is coincidence dressed as evidence.
distractors.C: Rebuilding from the nearest commit is the fallback if the archive is not self-contained, and it produces an approximation whose fidelity nobody can verify. Doing it before checking the archive risks spending the response window recreating something already held.
distractors.D: Accountability for the firm's own records sits with the firm, and provider-side retention may be short or contractually zero. Making the response depend on a third party's logs is both a weak evidentiary position and a slow one.

explanation.concept: When a reproducibility demand arrives, the first move is always to determine whether the existing record is self-contained, because that single fact decides whether the task is retrieval or forensic reconstruction. For probabilistic systems, the archived artefact - not a re-run - is the evidence.
explanation.tip: Next-step items reward sequencing. Options that start doing expensive work before establishing what is already known are almost always the trap, even when the work described is competent.

topic: SOC 2 Type II versus Type I in a vendor review
stem: A prospective enterprise customer asks for a SOC 2 Type II report covering your Claude-based platform rather than the Type I you already hold. What distinguishes the two?

options.text: A Type II examines whether controls operated effectively across a review period, while a Type I examines design suitability at a point in time.
A Type II report covers all five trust services criteria, while a Type I covers only the security criterion and its common controls.
A Type II report is issued by an independent audit firm, while a Type I is a self-assessment questionnaire published by the service organisation.
A Type II report extends the assessment to the organisation's subprocessors, while a Type I covers only systems the organisation operates itself.

explanation.correct: The distinction is time, not breadth. A point-in-time report can say the controls are sensibly designed; only an observation period can say they were actually operating - that access reviews really happened each quarter, that change approvals really were recorded. That is why enterprise buyers push for it and why the practical consequence for an architect is lead time: you cannot produce one retrospectively for a control you started running last week. Getting there means instrumenting evidence generation, such as automated logging of prompt-change approvals, well before the period opens.

distractors.B: Which trust services criteria are in scope is chosen when the engagement is defined and is independent of the report type. A Type I can cover several criteria and a Type II can be scoped to security alone.
distractors.C: Both types are attestation reports issued by an independent practitioner. Neither is a self-assessment, which is why buyers accept them at all; confusing this with a self-published questionnaire is a common procurement error.
distractors.D: How subservice organisations are treated is a scoping decision - carved out or included - made independently of the report type. Neither type automatically extends the audit boundary to vendors.

explanation.concept: Type I attests to control design at a moment; Type II attests to operating effectiveness across a period. For an AI platform this converts compliance into an engineering lead-time problem, because the evidence a Type II needs must be produced continuously by the system rather than assembled at audit time.
explanation.tip: If a stem tells you a customer is asking to upgrade from Type I to Type II, the underlying architectural point is nearly always evidence automation and the observation window, not documentation.

topic: Keeping the LLM path outside PCI DSS scope
stem: A travel booking platform wants a Claude agent to help support staff resolve payment disputes. The agent would read the booking record, the payment attempt history and the customer's message. Full primary account numbers currently appear in the payment attempt records. All prompts and completions pass through an internal model gateway and are written to a shared transcript store and a third-party tracing service, neither of which is segmented from the rest of the estate. The security architect must decide how to proceed before build starts.

options.text: Encrypt the transcript store and the tracing pipeline at rest with customer-managed keys, restrict access to a named support role, and treat those controls as removing both systems from cardholder data environment scope.
Add a system prompt rule instructing the model never to repeat a card number in its output, and monitor completions with an automated detector that redacts any match before it reaches the agent.

Accept the gateway, transcript store and tracing service into the cardholder data environment and complete the full assessment for all three, since any component supporting a payment workflow is in scope regardless of design.
Keep primary account numbers out of the prompt by passing a token that only an existing in-scope service can resolve, so the gateway, transcript store and tracing service never hold cardholder data.

explanation.correct: Scope follows the data. Once a full account number is placed in a prompt, every component that touches that prompt - the gateway, the transcript store and an external tracing vendor - is storing or transmitting cardholder data and is dragged into the assessment boundary along with everything they are not segmented from. The cheapest control by an order of magnitude is to keep the data out of the path: the agent reasons about a token and the last four digits, and any operation that genuinely needs the real number is executed by the existing in-scope service. The dispute workflow rarely needs the number itself, only the ability to act on it.

distractors.A: Encryption and access control are required controls for systems in scope; they are not a scope-removal mechanism. A system that stores encrypted cardholder data still stores cardholder data, and an unsegmented network pulls neighbouring systems in with it.
distractors.B: A prompt instruction is not a control an assessor can rely on, and it addresses only the output. The number has already been stored in the request payload, the transcript store and the trace, so scope has already attached before generation begins.
distractors.C: This is the over-scoping response, and it is expensive rather than wrong-headed. Assessment burden scales with the boundary, so an architecture that could have kept three systems out has instead committed the organisation to auditing them indefinitely.

explanation.concept: For payment data, the highest-leverage architectural decision is scope reduction: keep the regulated data element out of the LLM request path and give the model a reference it cannot dereference. Controls added around data you chose to admit are always more expensive than the decision not to admit it.
explanation.tip: In PCI-flavoured questions, look for the option that changes what enters the system rather than the option that hardens what the system does with it. Encryption-as-descoping is the classic wrong answer.

topic: Human review does not change an AI Act risk tier
stem: A pan-EU logistics group has two Claude-based tools nearing launch. The first ranks applicants for warehouse roles and surfaces a shortlist; a recruiter reviews every ranking and no candidate is rejected without a human clicking through. The second summarises supplier contracts for the in-house legal team. The general counsel argues that because a recruiter is always in the loop, the shortlisting tool avoids the heavier obligations under the EU AI Act. How should the architect frame the classification?

options.text: Because a recruiter reviews every ranking and no candidate is rejected without a human clicking through, the shortlisting tool falls outside the high-risk tier and owes only the transparency duties.

Classification follows the system's intended purpose, so a tool used to select candidates for employment sits in the high-risk tier; effective human oversight is an obligation that tier imposes, not an exit from it.
The contract summarisation tool carries the higher regulatory risk of the two, because it processes commercially sensitive third-party information and its errors can bind the company.
Risk tier is determined by the capability of the underlying general-purpose model, so the obligations sit with the model provider and the logistics group inherits them through its contract.

explanation.correct: The Act tiers systems by what they are used for and who is affected, and employment selection is squarely in the heavier tier because a wrong output costs a person a job. Human review is not an exit from that tier - it is one of the things the tier requires, which means the group must show the oversight is meaningful: the recruiter must have the information, the authority and the realistic capacity to disagree. A reviewer who approves ninety-eight percent of rankings in four seconds each is evidence that oversight is nominal, and that evidence will be read against the firm rather than for it.

distractors.A: This is the argument the stem invites you to accept. It inverts the logic: oversight is a control demanded of high-risk systems, so pointing at it concedes the classification rather than avoiding it, and rubber-stamp review makes the position worse.
distractors.C: Commercial sensitivity and contractual exposure are real risks, but they are risks to the company. Regulatory tiering keys on impact to people's fundamental rights, which is why an internal legal drafting aid sits far lower than a hiring filter.
distractors.D: Obligations are distributed across roles: whoever provides the general-purpose model has duties, and the organisation deploying it into a specific use has its own. A deployer cannot contract its way out of duties attached to the use it chose.

explanation.concept: Risk tiering under the EU AI Act is driven by intended purpose and the affected person's exposure, not by model capability, vendor identity or the presence of a human in the loop. Human oversight is an obligation inside the high-risk tier, and it must be demonstrably effective rather than procedurally present.
explanation.tip: Whenever a stem hands you 'but a human reviews it', check whether human review is being offered as an exemption. In regulated-AI questions it is almost always a requirement being mistaken for a defence.

topic: Transparency duty for systems that interact with people
stem: An organisation deploys a customer-facing Claude assistant to EU users. Which obligation attaches primarily because the system interacts directly with natural persons, rather than because of the risk tier its use case falls into?

options.text: A conformity assessment against the applicable requirements must be completed before the system is put into service.
The system must be entered in the relevant EU database before it is placed on the market or put into service.
People must be informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious in the circumstances.
A post-market monitoring plan must be maintained, with serious incidents reported to the market surveillance authority.

explanation.correct: Disclosure of AI interaction is the obligation that follows from the mode of interaction itself, which is why it can attach to a system whose use case is otherwise unremarkable. Architecturally it is cheap but easy to get wrong: the disclosure has to be visible at the point of interaction rather than buried in terms of service, and it has to survive channel changes, so an assistant reachable by chat, voice and email needs the disclosure in each. The 'unless obvious' carve-out is narrower than teams assume and is not satisfied by a robot avatar.

distractors.A: Conformity assessment belongs to the high-risk regime. A conversational assistant whose use case sits below that tier does not acquire the obligation merely by talking to customers.
distractors.B: Database registration is likewise a high-risk-tier duty tied to placing such systems on the market. It is not triggered by direct human interaction on its own.
distractors.D: Post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting are obligations of the heavier tier. They are good practice for any production AI system, but the stem asks which duty follows specifically from interacting with people.

explanation.concept: The EU AI Act layers obligations: some follow the risk tier of the use case, and a separate transparency layer follows from how the system engages people - disclosure of AI interaction, and marking of synthetic or manipulated content. A low-tier system can still owe transparency duties.
explanation.tip: When several options are all genuine obligations, the item is testing which trigger each one hangs off. Re-read the stem for the phrase that names the trigger - here, 'interacts directly with natural persons'.

topic: Core activities of an independent model validation
stem: A US regional bank must put its Claude-based commercial-loan memo drafting and covenant-risk flagging system through independent validation before it can leave pilot, under a model risk management framework of the SR 11-7 type. The model risk team is scoping the engagement. Which THREE activities are core to that validation? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: Obtaining sign-off from the development team lead confirming that the unit and integration test suites pass and the deployment pipeline is green.
Evaluating conceptual soundness: whether the design, prompt logic, retrieval sources and data suit the stated business purpose, with known limitations documented.
Establishing ongoing monitoring with defined performance thresholds, drift indicators and an escalation path once the system is live.
Negotiating commercial terms, capacity headroom and an uptime service level with the model provider before the system is approved for production.
Performing outcomes analysis, comparing system output against realised results or a benchmarked alternative on a held-out sample of loans.

explanation.correct: Validation frameworks of this kind rest on three legs, and an LLM system needs all three no less than a regression model does. Conceptual soundness asks whether this design can answer this question at all - for a generative system that means scrutinising the prompt, the retrieval corpus and the failure modes, not just the weights. Ongoing monitoring exists because a model that validated cleanly can degrade as portfolios and documents shift. Outcomes analysis is the empirical leg: compare what the system said against what actually happened or against a credible alternative. Drop any one and the validation is an opinion.

distractors.A: Engineering quality gates are necessary and unrelated. They test whether the software does what the developers intended, which is precisely the question independent validation is not allowed to take from the developers - independence is the point.
distractors.D: Commercial and availability terms belong to vendor management. They matter for resilience and are usually reviewed in parallel, but they say nothing about whether the model's outputs are fit for the decision they support.

explanation.concept: Independent validation has three pillars - conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, and outcomes analysis - performed by people with the standing to challenge the builders. Generative systems do not sit outside this: prompts, retrieval corpora and tool configurations are model components and fall inside the validation perimeter.
explanation.tip: In model risk questions, mentally sort each option into build, validate or operate. Anything a developer could sign for themselves is disqualified by the word 'independent' in the stem.

topic: Which vendors in an AI pipeline need business associate agreements
stem: A US telehealth provider generates clinical visit notes with Claude. The pipeline sends the visit transcript to the model provider, emits full request and response traces to a third-party observability vendor for latency debugging, and sends a weekly ten-percent sample of generated notes to an external clinical reviewer who scores accuracy under contract. Compliance is reviewing the arrangement before scale-up. What should the architect conclude?

options.text: Only the model provider requires a business associate agreement, since it is the only vendor performing a clinical function on the record rather than a supporting engineering one.
The observability vendor falls outside the requirement provided traces are sampled below a low threshold and are purged on a short retention clock enforced by the platform.

All three vendors - the model provider, the observability vendor and the scoring contractor - receive protected health information, so each needs its own business associate agreement and only the minimum data its function requires.

A business associate agreement with the model provider, combined with a flow-down clause obliging it to bind its own subcontractors and downstream processors, covers the full chain of vendors in this pipeline without separate agreements.

explanation.correct: The obligation follows the data, not the glamour of the function. Trace payloads in this design contain the transcript and the generated note, which makes the observability vendor a recipient of protected health information exactly as much as the model provider is, and the scoring contractor receives complete clinical notes by design. Each needs its own agreement. The second half matters just as much architecturally: latency debugging does not need the transcript body, so the trace can carry identifiers, timings and token counts with the payload omitted, which shrinks both the agreement burden and the breach surface.

distractors.A: This mistakes clinical significance for regulatory status. A vendor that stores a transcript in order to draw a latency chart holds the same data as one that generates a note from it, and the duty attaches to receiving the information on the covered entity's behalf.
distractors.B: Neither sampling rate nor retention period creates an exemption. Sampling reduces exposure and short retention reduces the window, but a single trace containing a patient's visit is still a disclosure requiring a governing agreement.
distractors.D: Flow-down obligations reach the model provider's own subcontractors. The observability vendor and the scoring contractor are the provider's own separate vendors, engaged directly, so nothing in that contract touches them.

explanation.concept: Map every hop that a regulated data element takes, including the ones added for engineering convenience: tracing, logging, evaluation, analytics and support tooling. Each hop that receives the data on your behalf needs its own contractual footing, and each is a candidate for payload reduction instead.
explanation.tip: Observability is the most commonly missed vendor in healthcare AI questions, because teams think of it as infrastructure rather than as a recipient of data. If a stem mentions full request and response traces, that vendor is in scope.

topic: Minimum necessary standard applied to prompt construction
stem: In a HIPAA-regulated Claude deployment, what does the minimum necessary standard most directly constrain about how prompts are built?

options.text: The amount of protected health information placed in each request must be limited to what that request's specific purpose needs.
Protected health information must be encrypted in transit and at rest wherever prompts are stored or transmitted.
Patient authorisation must be obtained before any protected health information is sent to an external vendor for processing.
Protected health information must be de-identified before it can be processed by any automated system, including a model endpoint.

explanation.correct: The standard bites directly on context assembly, which is where teams building LLM features tend to be most generous. Attaching the entire chart because it is one query away is the exact behaviour the rule is aimed at. In practice it pushes an architecture towards purpose-scoped retrieval - pulling the medication list for a medication question rather than the whole record - and it gives the design review a concrete question to ask of every field in the prompt template: what would break if this were removed.

distractors.B: Encryption obligations come from the security safeguards, and they apply to whatever data you have decided to process. They constrain protection, not volume, and a fully encrypted overshare is still an overshare.
distractors.C: Disclosures to a vendor performing a function on the covered entity's behalf are handled through a business associate arrangement rather than individual authorisation. Requiring authorisation for every vendor interaction would misstate the framework.
distractors.D: De-identification is one lawful route for some uses, notably research and analytics, but treatment and operations regularly require identified data. The standard limits how much is used, not whether identity may appear at all.

explanation.concept: Minimum necessary is a data-volume rule that lands squarely on context engineering: retrieve and include only the fields the task requires. It converts a compliance principle into a concrete prompt-design constraint, and it usually improves accuracy and cost at the same time.
explanation.tip: Compliance rules that constrain how much data you include tend to align with good context engineering. If an option describes protecting the data rather than reducing it, it is answering a different rule.

topic: Sourcing adverse action reasons from a generative system
stem: A US credit union runs a Claude step that reads an application file, summarises it for the underwriter, and drafts a fluent paragraph explaining why the application looks weak. The actual approve or decline outcome is produced by a separate deterministic scorecard plus policy rules. Product proposes sending the model's paragraph to declined applicants as the adverse action notice, arguing it is clearer than the current reason codes. What position should the architect take?

options.text: The paragraph may be sent as written provided an underwriter reads and initials it before dispatch, since documented human review satisfies the accuracy requirement.
The disclosed reasons must come from the factors that actually drove the scorecard and rules outcome; the model may re-render a derived reason in plainer language but cannot be its source.
Having the model select from a fixed taxonomy of compliance-approved reason codes resolves the problem, because the wording of every code has already been reviewed.
The requirement is met by disclosing in the notice which model and version produced the assessment, together with an offer to explain the decision further on request.

explanation.correct: The decision here is made by the scorecard and the rules, so the true principal reasons are recoverable from them. A paragraph generated from a file summary is a plausible narrative about a decision it did not make, and plausible-but-wrong is the worst possible failure for a notice that the applicant may act on and a regulator may test. The clean architecture separates the two jobs: derive the reasons deterministically from the decisioning logic, then optionally use the model to phrase them in readable English, with the derived reason as an input the model may not contradict.

distractors.A: Human review of a rationalisation checks whether it reads well, not whether it corresponds to the mechanism that produced the outcome. Underwriters reviewing at volume will approve fluent text, and a wrong reason approved by a person is still a wrong reason.
distractors.C: Pre-approved wording fixes the language and leaves the hard part untouched. If the model picks the code from a summary rather than from the scorecard's factor contributions, it can still select an accurate-sounding code that is not what actually drove the decline.
distractors.D: Naming the model discloses the tool, not the reasons. An applicant who is told which system assessed them still has no idea what to change, which is the whole purpose of the requirement.

explanation.concept: When a deterministic component makes the decision and a generative component describes it, the disclosure must be sourced from the decider and only rendered by the describer. Never let an explanation-generating model become the system of record for why an outcome occurred.
explanation.tip: Look for stems that quietly separate 'the model summarises' from 'a scorecard decides'. That separation is the whole item: the explanation has to come from wherever the decision came from.

topic: Operational consequences of a zero-retention arrangement
stem: A Swiss private bank has negotiated a zero-retention arrangement with its model provider: no prompt or completion is persisted on the provider side beyond the life of the request. The head of technology risk asks the architect what this changes about the design of the surrounding platform. What is the most important consequence?

options.text: Because nothing is retained by the provider, the bank no longer needs its own retention schedule for AI interactions and can fold them into its general records policy.
Because no copy persists at the provider, the interaction data is effectively anonymous once the response is returned, so subject access and erasure rights no longer attach to it.
Every artefact the bank may later need - incident forensics, abuse investigation, evaluation corpora, regulatory evidence - must now be captured and protected on the bank's own side.
Because the data never persists outside the request, cross-border transfer analysis for the inference call becomes unnecessary and the destination need not appear in the transfer register.

explanation.correct: Zero retention moves work rather than removing it. Every reason someone might reach for provider-side logs - reconstructing an incident, investigating a misuse pattern, assembling a regression set, showing a supervisor what happened - now has to be satisfied from the bank's own capture, which means that capture has to exist, be complete enough, and be protected well enough to be trusted. Teams that adopt zero retention as a purely contractual win and change nothing architecturally discover the gap during their first incident, when there is nothing to go back to on either side.

distractors.A: This inverts the consequence. The bank's retention obligations arise from its own regulatory and evidential needs, and zero retention at the provider makes the bank's own schedule more load-bearing, not less.
distractors.B: Anonymity is a property of the data, not of how long a third party keeps it. The prompt still contains identifiable client information while it is being processed, and the bank's own copies remain fully in scope for individual rights.
distractors.D: Processing still occurs wherever the inference runs, and transient processing is still processing. Retention duration affects the risk profile of a transfer; it does not remove the need to establish the transfer's legal footing.

explanation.concept: A zero data retention commitment is a boundary condition, not a compliance outcome. It removes third-party copies and simultaneously removes third-party recourse, so the controller must own capture, protection and retention for every downstream need it previously assumed someone else could serve.
explanation.tip: Ask what capability you are giving up alongside the risk you are removing. Zero retention questions almost always key on the loss of forensic and evaluation material rather than on the privacy benefit.

topic: Sequencing a decision to route inference outside the EEA
stem: A Brazilian retail group's German subsidiary runs a Claude-based product-advice assistant for EU shoppers. Capacity in the current in-region deployment is tight ahead of a seasonal peak eight weeks away, and the platform team proposes repointing a share of traffic to a non-EEA region where headroom exists. The subsidiary's DPO has flagged the change as a cross-border transfer. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Test whether in-region capacity can be expanded to cover the peak, since removing the transfer costs less than justifying one; only if it cannot should a transfer mechanism and assessment be completed first.
Repoint the traffic now to protect the peak, and add the new destination region to the record of processing activities and the customer privacy notice at the next quarterly governance review.

Pseudonymise customer identifiers in the prompt by replacing the customer number with a lookup token before transmission, so the transferred payload is no longer personal data and the transfer question does not arise.
Adopt the model provider's published certifications for the destination region as the transfer mechanism, on the basis that the provider has already addressed the destination's legal environment.

explanation.correct: Eight weeks is enough time to solve this either way, which makes it worth solving in the order that costs least. A transfer needs a mechanism, an assessment of the destination, supplementary measures where the assessment demands them, and updated notices and records - all of which is durable overhead on every future release. Additional in-region capacity, if it exists, removes the entire workstream. The step is diagnostic rather than a refusal: if in-region genuinely cannot absorb the peak, the team then has seven weeks to do the transfer work properly rather than retrofitting it.

distractors.B: Sequencing is the failure here. Moving personal data first and documenting later means the transfer happens without a mechanism in place, and a quarterly review is far too slow a control loop for a change of this kind.
distractors.C: Pseudonymised data remains personal data as long as re-identification is possible with additional information, and shopping context frequently carries identifying detail regardless of whether the customer number is masked. This defers the problem rather than removing it.
distractors.D: A provider's certifications describe the provider's own controls. The transfer mechanism and the assessment behind it are the controller's responsibility, and outsourcing that judgement to a vendor's marketing collateral is not a defensible position.

explanation.concept: Treat cross-border routing as an architectural choice with a permanent compliance cost, and test whether the requirement can be met without the transfer before designing around it. Data residency is far cheaper to preserve than to re-establish once traffic has moved.
explanation.tip: When a stem gives you a comfortable lead time, it is usually signalling that the fast option is a trap. The right first step in transfer questions is almost always to test whether the transfer is avoidable.

topic: Making an AI decision log tamper-evident
stem: An AI decision log must let an auditor demonstrate, after the fact, that no entry was altered or silently removed. Which property most directly provides that?

options.text: Write access to the log is restricted to a small group of platform operators authenticated with hardware security tokens.
Each record is sealed with a hash covering the preceding record, so alteration or deletion breaks a chain an auditor can recompute.
The log is replicated synchronously across three availability zones with automatic failover and periodic restore testing.
Records are written asynchronously through a durable queue, so an application failure can never block or drop entries on the logging path.

explanation.correct: Tamper evidence is about detection by an independent party, and chaining each record to its predecessor gives exactly that: recomputing the chain either reproduces the published value or it does not, and the check works without trusting the operator of the store. It also catches deletion, which pure integrity hashes on individual records do not, because removing a link breaks the sequence. Publishing the chain head periodically to a separate custody domain strengthens it further by removing the possibility of a wholesale consistent rewrite.

distractors.A: Access control reduces who can tamper. It provides no way to demonstrate afterwards that nobody did, and it offers nothing against the privileged insider or the compromised operator account that auditors are most interested in.
distractors.C: Replication protects availability and durability. Three faithful copies of a record that was altered before it was written, or altered everywhere at once, are three copies of the same problem.
distractors.D: Asynchronous writing improves availability of the logging path and reduces the chance of gaps caused by application failure. It says nothing about whether a record already written can be changed.

explanation.concept: Distinguish tamper-resistance, which makes alteration hard, from tamper-evidence, which makes alteration provable. Audit logs for regulated AI decisions need the second: cryptographic chaining, with the chain head periodically anchored outside the control of whoever runs the store.
explanation.tip: Read the verb in the stem. 'Prevent' points at access control and write-once storage; 'demonstrate' or 'prove after the fact' points at cryptographic chaining.

topic: Legal hold overriding an automated retention expiry job
stem: A media company's Claude-based content moderation system stores the prompt, retrieved policy context and decision for every review, and a nightly job deletes those records after thirty days under the published retention schedule. Litigation has now been filed and counsel has issued a preservation hold covering moderation decisions for a specific set of eleven creator accounts, going forward and back. The platform team must respond this week. What should the architect implement?

options.text: Suspend the expiry job across the entire corpus until the matter concludes, since selective suspension risks missing responsive records and creating spoliation exposure.
Let the nightly schedule continue to run, on the basis that consistent application of a published retention policy is itself the defence to a preservation challenge.
Add a per-record hold attribute that the expiry job checks before deleting, so records for the eleven accounts are preserved indefinitely while the rest of the corpus ages out on schedule.
Export a summary spreadsheet of the affected moderation outcomes to a separate legal archive and allow the primary records to expire, treating the export as the preserved copy.

explanation.correct: A hold and a retention schedule are not in conflict if the store can express scope. Marking the eleven accounts and having the expiry job honour that mark preserves precisely what must be preserved and nothing else, which satisfies counsel without turning a thirty-day corpus into an indefinite one for millions of unrelated creators. The forward-looking half matters equally: new records for those accounts must be created already marked, so the hold has to be applied at write time and not only as a one-off sweep over what exists today.

distractors.A: Freezing everything is over-collection dressed as caution. It contradicts the company's own minimisation position, balloons storage and exposure, and creates a much larger discovery surface than the matter requires.
distractors.B: Routine, consistently applied retention is a reasonable posture until a preservation obligation attaches. Once it does, continuing to delete responsive records is the classic spoliation fact pattern, and the policy becomes an aggravating detail rather than a defence.
distractors.D: A summary is lossy. The prompt, the retrieved policy context and the model's output are the evidence, and a spreadsheet of outcomes discards exactly the material that would show how each decision was reached.

explanation.concept: Retention automation must be designed with an override channel from day one: a per-record or per-subject hold flag that every expiry path consults, applied both retrospectively and at write time. Systems whose only retention control is a blanket time-to-live force a choice between deleting evidence and keeping everything.
explanation.tip: Preservation questions test granularity. Options that suspend deletion globally and options that keep deleting are both wrong; the answer is nearly always scoped hold with the schedule left running elsewhere.

topic: Purpose limitation when production transcripts become eval data
stem: A Spanish telco wants to build a permanent regression evaluation set from real customer-service transcripts handled by its Claude assistant, so that prompt changes can be gated on realistic cases. Privacy counsel has raised purpose limitation: the transcripts were collected to service customers, not to test software. Which TWO steps most directly address that objection? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Encrypt the evaluation store with customer-managed keys held in the telco's own key management service and rotate them on a fixed schedule.
Record a compatibility assessment for the secondary use, or establish a separate basis for it, and reflect the evaluation purpose in the processing record and the privacy notice.
Keep the evaluation set inside the production transcript database under the same retention clock, so that the secondary use inherits the primary purpose and needs no separate governance.
Obtain fresh explicit consent from every customer whose transcript is selected, since consent is the only basis that can support a secondary use of data already collected.
Reduce the corpus to the minimum number of cases needed for coverage and strip direct identifiers and irrelevant content from each transcript before it enters the evaluation store.

explanation.correct: Purpose limitation is answered by two moves. First, do the analysis and write it down: either the new purpose is compatible with the original one - which turns on the relationship with the customer, their reasonable expectations, the sensitivity of the content and the safeguards applied - or it needs its own basis, and either way it belongs in the processing record and the notice. Second, apply the safeguards that make compatibility defensible, because minimisation and identifier removal are not merely hygiene here; they are the factors the assessment itself weighs. Together they turn an assertion into a documented position.

distractors.A: Encryption at rest with controlled keys is a sound security control and does nothing for purpose limitation. The question is whether the telco may use the data for this purpose at all, not how well the copy is protected once made.
distractors.C: Co-locating the eval set with production data does not merge the purposes; it obscures them, and it means the eval set silently ages out under a retention clock set for a different purpose. A regression suite that deletes itself every ninety days is also useless.
distractors.D: Consent is one possible basis among several and is a poor fit here - it is impractical at corpus scale, and a set that shrinks whenever consent is withdrawn is not a stable regression baseline. Framing it as the only option misstates the framework.

explanation.concept: Reusing production data for evaluation is a change of purpose, not a change of storage location. Handle it with an explicit compatibility analysis plus real safeguards - minimisation, identifier removal, access restriction and a purpose-specific retention rule - and register the eval corpus as a processing activity in its own right.
explanation.tip: Multi-select privacy items often mix genuine security controls in with the answer. Encryption and key management are almost never the response to a purpose or basis objection; they answer a confidentiality objection instead.
